Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-23
Time: 15:00 - 15:45 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Cypress Product), Priya Singh (Cypress Eng), Markus Vogel (Cypress Security)

Optional auto sections:
Summary: quick sync on app integration: SDK usage, function/tool calling, structured output. agreed next steps to run benches and share docs.
Topics: see topics above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sam: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Real quick, agenda  SDK snippet review, the function call flow you tried last week, structured output schema, and security questions. Anything else?
[00:10] Jordan: No, that covers it, Sam. We mostly want to see if the SDK integration is producing stable, parseable JSON and whether the latency numbers still look ok for in-app use.
[00:20] Priya: And also to check edge cases where the model returns partially malformed JSON, we need to know best recoveries.
[00:30] Maya: Cool; I'll jump into the SDK bits. Quick note  we pushed a small update to the JS/TS SDK last night that adds function-calling helpers and a structured-output validator. It's not a breaking change but it should help with the parsing retries.
[00:45] Priya: Nice. Did you also add the streaming fallback for large responses? We saw some timeouts with longer records.
[00:52] Maya: Yup  streaming + chunked structured output. It emits partial JSON chunks and a final validation step. There are some caveats if your client times out early.
[01:05] Jordan: When you say function calling helpers, is that the SDK automatically mapping tools to function signatures or is it opt-in by route?
[01:15] Maya: Opt-in. You provide the tool list and signature in the call, SDK does the serialization; there's an example where we wrap your internal patient-search API as a tool and the model returns a call object. We convert that into a function invocation in the app.
[01:30] Sam: Real quick  we actually recorded a small demo of the flow with Cypress's sample prompt set. Sam: I'll send the snippet after the call.
[01:42] Priya: Perfect. The problem we had last week was twofold: 1) model sometimes returns near-matching keys like "patient_id" vs "patientId" and 2) partial JSON when the token limit cuts off.
[01:55] Maya: For the key normalization, we added a tolerant deserializer option that maps common variants and a schema-guided fallback. For partial JSON we recommend the SDK's re-ask pattern: on invalid JSON, return the last prompt prefix + error trace and ask the model to finish the JSON only. It tends to be much cheaper than re-running from scratch.
[02:12] Jordan: How do we instrument that? We need traces to see how often re-asks happen.
[02:20] Maya: The SDK emits structured events  call.start, call.tool.invoke, call.finish, validation.error  those go to your observability endpoint or our Console. We can show token usage and where re-asks happen.
[02:30] Markus: From security perspective, we need to know what gets logged. The observability events  do they include PII? We cannot send patient identifiers off-prem.
[02:40] Sam: Good call. For PII you can opt-out of payload logging in Redwood Console and use client-side masking. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and VPC-only egress; logs can be kept in your S3 with encryption.
[02:55] Markus: Are those docs ready? Our compliance team wants SOC2 artifacts and an example KMS config.
[03:03] Maya: We have the SOC2 + architecture whitepaper. I'll attach the KMS/HSM integration guide. There's also a short VPC runbook.
[03:12] Sam: We'll share those after the call  link in the follow-up.
[03:18] Priya: Back to perf  we ran a small bench with your hosted API and saw p95 generation latency around 420ms for typical 100-token responses, but cost was higher than we expected. If we move to Dedicated it should drop but we need numbers on throughput and queueing.
[03:33] Maya: Right  Dedicated gives you lower p95 and higher concurrent throughput because you get reserved GPU pools. There's a tradeoff: cost per hour vs per-token price. For your workload (short responses, high QPS) Dedicated often wins on latency and predictable tail. We can run a 1k-message bench with both hosted fallbacks and Dedicated routing and show token cost and p95.
[03:54] Jordan: That would be great. Also, how do fallbacks work? If Dedicated is saturated, do requests go to hosted automatically?
[04:02] Sam: You can configure routing policy: strict (reject when no Dedicated capacity) or graceful fallback (route to hosted or compatible quantized model). We recommend graceful for customer-facing flows.
[04:12] Priya: For our gut feeling on cost, can the SDK batch similar calls across users? We have an ephemeral chat flow.
[04:20] Maya: There's automatic batching at the runtime layer  it aggregates small calls into micro-batches where latency budget allows. The SDK exposes hints like latency_budget_ms to tune batching behavior.
[04:30] Priya: We'll want to tune that.
[04:35] Jordan: On structured output  we tried the schema you suggested but the model inserted extra fields occasionally which broke downstream parsers.
[04:45] Maya: Two strategies: strict schema enforcement (model forced to return only allowed keys) or tolerant parser that ignores unknown keys. We typically recommend enforcing the schema at the model layer for critical fields and tolerant parsing for optional metadata.
[04:58] Priya: Does the SDK support auto-coercion? e.g., string "age" to integer?
[05:05] Maya: Yes, simple coercion rules are included. Edge cases may require a lightweight post-process hook. We can add a code sample in the snippet.
[05:14] Jordan: Can we see an example of function + structured output together? Last time the model returned a function call with JSON args that included nested patient info and then included a free-text explanation  parsing that was messy.
[05:27] Maya: Sure  typical pattern: the model returns {"tool_call": {"name": "patient_search", "args": {...}}} then a separate "response" field for human-facing text. The SDK splits those into a tool invocation event and a final normalized response. We'll include the example in the snippet.
[05:45] Sam: I'll drop an example after the call.
[05:50] Markus: Quick legal/security question  when the model calls a tool that queries our internal DB, that call happens inside the VPC if we use Private deployment, right? So data doesn't leave the VPC?
[06:00] Maya: Correct. With Private you can run the entire runtime inside your VPC and Redwood's control plane only handles orchestration; no data egress unless you opt in.
[06:09] Markus: Good. For the POC we might start with hosted but with logs scrubbed. Then if things look good move to a Private pilot.
[06:18] Sam: That's a common path.
[06:20] Jordan: Any blockers from Redwood's side to run the bench?
[06:25] Maya: We just need your typical prompt patterns and a small sample dataset (anonymized) so we can reproduce. Also confirm target QPS and latency SLO.
[06:35] Priya: We'll send prompt templates and a 500-row anonymized sample by Monday.
[06:40] Jordan: Timeline  can you run bench and send results the week after?
[06:44] Maya: Yes, we'll aim for sending initial bench by Jan 5.
[06:48] Sam: Anything else?
[06:50] Jordan: One more  error handling on function calls: if the tool returns 500, what's the recommended pattern? Retry? Fallback to a simpler model?
[06:58] Maya: For transient tool errors, we recommend an exponential backoff + quick re-ask to the model to decide alternative strategies (like partial results). If the tool is down we have routing rules to call a degraded search model or fallback cache.
[07:12] Priya: Ok, that helps.
[07:15] Jordan: Can we get the SDK sample in both Node and Python? Our backend is Python but a small client is Node.
[07:22] Sam: Yes  we'll include both.
[07:25] Maya: Also note the SDK has a thin adapter for your existing HTTP client so you don't have to rip out code.
[07:30] Priya: Nice.
[07:32] Markus: Security follow-up  we'll want to review the SOC2 evidence and KMS integration before we open up any patient-like data, even anonymized.
[07:40] Sam: Understood  we'll attach those docs and propose a security deep dive next week.
[07:46] Jordan: Sounds good.
[07:48] Sam: Recap  Sam to send SDK snippets (Node + Python) with structured output + function-call examples; Maya to run Dedicated vs Hosted bench and share spreadsheet; Cypress to send prompts and sample dataset; Redwood to share SOC2/KMS/VPC docs; schedule security deep-dive.
[08:05] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[08:08] Markus: Thanks.
[08:10] Sam: We'll follow up via email and log action items in the CRM. Bye all.
